CASE 06 · FRACTURE CARE

Fracture above the knee fixed with a locking plate

A multi-fragment fracture of the lower thigh bone, just above the knee, rebuilt with a locking plate and screws. The X-rays, the surgery and the healing timeline.

  • Area: Lower femur, above the knee
  • Procedure: Locking plate fixation (ORIF)
  • Bone healing: 12–16 weeks
Read the case ↓

The distal femur is the lower end of the thigh bone, where it widens to form the top of the knee joint. Fractures here usually follow a road traffic accident or a fall from a height. In older people with weaker bone, a simple fall can be enough. Because the break lies so close to the knee, accurate repair is essential for walking and knee movement later.

Condition
Comminuted distal femur (supracondylar) fracture
Treatment
Open reduction and internal fixation with a locking plate
Knee movement
Starts within days
Hospital stay
Usually 5–7 days
Bone healing
About 12–16 weeks (up to 6 months)
Final result
6–12 months

Tap or click an image to view it full size.

01

What the “before” X-ray shows

The front view of the knee and lower thigh shows a complex fracture:

  • A fracture just above the knee (supracondylar): the femur has broken in the widened lower part of the bone, just above the knee joint.
  • Multiple fragments (comminution): rather than a single clean break, the bone has split into several pieces, including a long, sharp spike of the shaft.
  • Fracture lines heading towards the joint: lines extend down towards the area between the two femoral condyles (the rounded ends that form the knee joint), so the joint block must be rebuilt as well as the shaft.
  • Shin bone intact: the tibia and the knee joint below the fracture are not broken, which helps the knee recover once the femur heals.
02

Why surgery was needed

A fracture this unstable cannot be held in plaster. Without surgery the leg would shorten and angle, and the knee would stiffen. Internal fixation restores length, alignment and rotation, and allows the knee to start moving within days.

03

The procedure

The operation is called open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF):

  • Rebuild the joint end first: the condyles are aligned and held with screws across the knee end of the bone.
  • Reconnect to the shaft: the rebuilt joint block is then attached to the shaft, restoring the correct length, angle and rotation of the leg.
  • Locking plate: a long plate shaped to the outer femur is fixed with locking screws, which thread into the plate itself and form a rigid, fixed-angle frame. This holds firmly even in multi-fragment fractures or weaker bone.
04

What the “after” X-ray confirms

The post-operative image shows:

  • Plate position: the plate runs along the outer side of the lower femur, sitting well on the bone from the knee end up the shaft.
  • Multiple screws across the condyles: these hold the knee end of the bone together as one solid block.
  • Screws into the shaft: spaced screws above the fracture zone anchor the plate to healthy bone.
  • Restored alignment: the femur is back to its normal length and straight line over the knee joint, which remains well preserved.
  • Surgical drain: the thin curved tube on the outer thigh is a temporary drain, usually removed within 24–48 hours.

Recovery and healing timeline

Every recovery is individual. These are the typical stages, and your own plan will be adjusted at each follow-up visit.

Wound healingAbout 2 weeksStitches or staples out at 12–14 days
Bone healingAbout 12–16 weeksUp to 6 months for complex breaks
Full recoveryAbout 6–12 monthsStrength and walking pattern
  1. Days 1–3

    Early knee movement

    Thigh-muscle tightening and gentle knee bending start immediately. Patients sit up and stand with a walker, keeping weight off the operated leg (or only light toe-touch) as advised.

  2. Days 4–7

    Discharge home

    Once walking safely with the walker without putting weight on the leg, patients go home, usually within 5–7 days. Blood-clot prevention continues as prescribed.

  3. Week 2

    Wound check

    Stitches or staples are removed. The goal is to bend the knee to at least 90° by about 4–6 weeks.

  4. Weeks 2–6

    Protected walking

    Walking with a walker or crutches, without full weight on the leg. Daily exercises keep the knee moving and the muscles active.

  5. Weeks 6–10

    Partial weight-bearing

    When follow-up X-rays show early new bone (callus), weight on the leg is increased gradually under the surgeon’s guidance.

  6. Weeks 10–16

    Full weight-bearing

    As the fracture unites, most patients progress to full weight and then to a stick. Complex, multi-fragment fractures can take up to 5–6 months to heal completely.

  7. Months 6–12

    Full recovery

    Muscle strength, knee bend and a normal walking pattern continue to improve. The plate usually stays in permanently unless it causes problems.

05

Helping your recovery at home

  • Do not put more weight on the leg than advised; early overloading can bend or break the fixation.
  • Keep the knee moving daily; stiffness is the biggest risk after fractures near the knee.
  • Take blood-clot prevention medicine for as long as prescribed.
  • A diet with enough protein, calcium and vitamin D supports bone healing. Avoid smoking, which slows it.

When to contact the clinic urgently

  • Fever, or increasing redness, warmth or discharge from the wound
  • Calf pain or swelling, or sudden chest pain or breathlessness (seek emergency care)
  • New numbness, tingling, or a cold or pale limb
  • A sudden increase in pain, a new deformity, or being unable to move or bear weight as before
